*The Compendium of the Meaning of the Siddhānta*, p. 57):
Homage to the two feet of the venerable Padmarasarāja, who is worthy of worship.
The Compendium of the Meaning of the Siddhānta:
By him who is omniscient and eternally manifest, through compassion, knowledge was revealed for the sake of destroying the bonds of beginningless impurity and the like for those bound souls.
Having bowed to that supreme Śiva, the supreme Guru, and all other gurus,
this compendium of the meaning of the Siddhānta, obtained from the mouth of the Guru, is clearly written down.
And no authority is established there in various ways,
since it is seen in all the Śiva scriptures as well as in their commentaries.
Therefore, that very meaning which has been determined by the most excellent teachers through both scripture and reasoning is here presented by us in brief.

In that regard, the supreme knowledge of the Lord is of two forms: the form of consciousness (*avabodha*) and the form of sound (*śabda*). Among these, the form of consciousness is stainless, without beginning or end, the illuminator of all objects, the bestower of grace upon all, and consists of the knowledge of Śiva. The form of sound, however, consists precisely of the scriptures. Furthermore, as for the form of consciousness...

The Supreme Lord, who is supremely compassionate, at the time of every creation, out of a desire to favor all beings, imparts [the teaching] to those who are worthy through the lineage of gurus, having mounted it upon the form of words. As it is said in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
Then, for the sake of liberation from the bondage of karma known as the impurity of the self consisting of māyā,
and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva, knowledge proceeds from Śiva.
And in the *Mokṣakārikā*:
"Although it has been established from beginningless time within Śaṅkara as being his quality...
And that which correctly discerns this is declared to be the knowledge of Śaṅkara.

The lineage of the succession of gurus is twofold: characterized by the Great Current (mahaugha) and characterized by the individual compendia of the gurus (pratisaṃhita). Among these, that characterized by the Great Current is now demonstrated. Therein, the Supreme Lord, having first bestowed grace upon the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), [transmitted] twenty-eight compendia (saṃhitās) to them.
He reveals it. Furthermore, they—in the sequence beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with sages and humans—bring down all the Saṃhitās.
This is the descent of the scripture, characterized by the great current (mahaugha). As it is said in the venerable Mālinīvijaya:
Desirous of creating the world, at the very beginning of creation, by his own will,
he awakened eight *pudgala*s known as *vijñānakevala*s.
And this lineage of gurus (gurukrama) is heard of in the venerable Raurava and other scriptures:
"The supreme Guru, the Lord Analeśa, is the cause of the universe;
that which was spoken by the Supreme Lord was [then] taught to the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha. Thus it is said.
This knowledge was uttered by Śiva and received by the lords of the lords of mantras;
because it grants all desires, it is celebrated at great length as the Kāmika.
Having learned from them that the tree of Smara was firmly consumed by the rows of flames of the light of his vision,
the Lord of Umā said to me, "Become [one with] thousands equal to Bhava. Thus, the lineage of the Gurus is presented in its entirety, as it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
Immediately after creation, the Lord Śiva, having created ten sons,
quickly divided the single knowledge into as many parts as there were sons and spoke it to them.
The power of the one called *praṇava* is *kāmika*; that of the one called *sudhā* is born of yoga;
that of the one called *dīpta* is inconceivable; and that of the one called *kāraṇa* is the ultimate cause. (p. 59)
The Ajita belongs to the Lord known as Suśiva, and the Sudīptaka also belongs to him.
The subtle [kalpa] belongs to Sūkṣmasaṃjña; the thousandfold [kalpa] belongs to Kāla;
the Suprabha belongs to Gaṇeśa; and the Aṃśumat belongs to Aṃśusaṃjña.
Thus the first [lineage] has been declared; now there is another sequence of gurus:
Praṇava obtained Kāmika from Trikala, and Hara [obtained it] from Trikala.
From Sudhākhyā was born the Tantra; from that came the Lord known as Bhasma;
from Dīpta came the Inconceivable (Acintya); and from that came Gopati and then Ambikā.
From Kāraṇa, Śarva obtained it; from him, Prajāpati received it;
from Suśiva, Ajita obtained it; and from Umēśa, Acyuta received it.
From Īśa, the radiant Trimūrti was obtained; from him, Hutāśana (Fire) was obtained;
from the Subtle (Sūkṣma), Sūkṣmābhava (the subtle-born) was obtained; and from him, Prabhañjana (Wind) was obtained.
From Kālasaṃjña came Sahasrākhya; from him, O bird, came Bhīma; from Dharmas then came Gaṇeśa; from Gaṇeśa came Suprabheda; and from Vigraheśa came Śaśin.
From Aṃśusaṃjña came Aṃśumat, and from him was obtained the fierce Ravi;
thus these ten divisions of Śiva have been fully described.
Another distinct division of Rudras, numbering eighteen, is also recognized;
for, having previously created the Rudras by the number eighteen from his eastern face and the others.
O Bird, Śiva would then awaken them again by that very number, with [the words] beginning:
"The victory of Rudra, whose name is Anādi, has been proclaimed by him," and so forth (p.

"Up to the end of the statement, 'No difference in fruit is to be imagined here; rather, a difference in knowledge is postulated,' the meaning is as follows: the Tantras are twofold, distinguished by the division into the Śiva-bheda and the Rudra-bheda. Among these, the Śiva-bheda [bestows grace] upon those residing in the Sadāśiva-tattva, having favored them with the *praṇava* and so forth."

Having fashioned for them a single knowledge whose nature is awakening, He taught it by dividing it tenfold— according to their respective capacities— through the arrangement of words and preceded by creation, distinguished by [the categories of] action and so forth. Having favored the eighteen Rudras, beginning with the divisions of Rudra such as Tanu and the rest, who were already endowed with knowledge, He [taught] the arrangement of words.

Having done so, it was likewise revealed through the eighteenfold division of tantras beginning with the *Vijaya*. And those Rudras reside below the principle (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva. For this very reason, the supreme and inferior nature of the divisions of Śiva and the divisions of Rudra is stated in the venerable *Svacchanda Tantra*:
The entire [text], however, was arranged by the gods, beginning with Oṃkāra, in due order;
thus it is said that the eighteen Rudras constitute the Brāhma [portion]. Furthermore, even regarding those two, a distinction between students (*adhyetṛ*) and teachers (*pravaktṛ*) has been stated.
Even among these various divisions, because of the differences among students and the differences among teachers, it is impossible to state [a definitive] division. Therefore, of this...

The distinction [in Śiva-jñāna] arises from the different modes of its descent and from the differences in ritual action (*kriyā*), but not from a difference in the established nature of the object (*artha*) nor from a difference in the fruit (*phala*). As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Śiva-jñāna is indeed one alone, yet it is further divided tenfold."
Likewise, it is further expanded through eighteen distinct divisions.
The single knowledge of Śiva is again divided in many ways;
there is no end to its sub-divisions and further sub-divisions.
All other varieties [of initiation], whether they be great or not great,
serve the purpose of providing conviction and have both supernatural power (siddhi) and liberation (mukti) as their fruits.

61) Others also say: "The ritual act is one and the same, as evidenced by all the Vedic branches. Regarding these various systems (tantra), the connection with the lineage of gurus is in some cases fivefold and in others sixfold.

As stated by the venerable Mataṅga, [the connection] is of five kinds. To explain: the connection between Śiva and Ananta is *para* (supreme); that between Ananta and Śrīkaṇṭha is *mahat* (great); that between Śrīkaṇṭha and Mataṅga is *divya* (divine); that between the sage Mataṅga and human beings is *divyādivya* (divine-cum-non-divine); and that among human beings themselves is [the fifth].
For human beings, it is non-divine in nature. However, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, it is of six kinds, as follows:
the supreme relationship between Śiva and Ananta; the great [relationship] between Ananta and Śrīkaṇṭha;
the intermediate-inferior [relationship] between Śrīkaṇṭha and Śakra; the divine [relationship] between Śakra and Bharadvāja; and [the relationship] of Bharadvāja...

Among the two Hārītas, one is divine and the other is non-divine; likewise, among the disciples of Hārīta, there is one who is non-divine. I consider that this should be understood accordingly even in other cases.

Thus, because the tradition of the lineage of gurus is remembered as being unbroken up to the Supreme Lord (Āparameśvara), the authority of this scripture is established by virtue of its being composed by Him. As it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
"That single authoritative statement is the reality spoken by the Lord.

Now, some maintain that the authority of scripture (*āgama*) derives from its eternity; however, this is incorrect, because this scripture is possible to be produced, since it possesses composition, like a sentence newly composed. And that composition is like that of a bridge and so forth. Of that...
It does not deviate from its author; therefore, the authority of scripture (āgama) rests solely upon its being composed by a reliable person (āpta).

And the Supreme Lord is the supreme reliable person, because He is endowed with eternal, pure, and unsurpassed knowledge and action regarding all objects, because deception is impossible due to the absence of passion and hatred, and because He is the benefactor of all.

As it is stated in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*: "Whatever object exists in whatever manner, the Omniscient One would describe it exactly as it is. And God is established through both direct perception and inference.

For thus it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: having first described the attainment of the Lord (*īśvara-siddhi*) preceded by the attainment of power (*śakti-siddhi*), it is said that [the Lord] is accessible through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa-gamya*) of the yogin:
"O best of sages, he is either empowered (*śakta*), possessed of power (*śaktimān*), or even accomplished (*siddha*)."
The senses are each individually perceptual, and the mind is the unsurpassed sense.
O tiger among sages, that which is to be attained is accomplished solely through resolve, having resolve as its object; what else do you wish to ask?

Thus, it should not be said that [the existence] of yogins is unestablished; for it is heard in scripture: "Making the self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, through the practice of churning with knowledge, one shall behold the God as if hidden."

The fact that [the existence of God] is established through inference is also stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra* and other texts: "Now, having perceived the body and so forth as things possessing the property of being effects,
we know their agent to be distinguished [from ordinary beings] by means of inference."
The distinction [of the cause] is observed even in worldly affairs through the distinction of the effect;
its establishment by scripture is also stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "The glorious *sakala* is recited as having the body of the five mantras."
With a perfectly serene collection of sense-faculties, he is omniscient and the range of all things.
"The Lord is the master of yoga, independent, and the destroyer of the bonds of the bound (paśu);
His teaching is not sublated by gross human means of knowledge.
Since this proof of the Lord has been established in detail in all the Saṃhitās and in the Nyāsa texts and so forth, it is not treated here.

It is written: Nor should the fault of mutual dependence be suspected regarding the establishment of God from a scripture created by God, because both [the scripture and the act of creation] possess dissimilar modes of operation.

For God is the author of the scripture (*āgama*), and the scripture makes Him known. Furthermore, since one observes that those matters of perceived reality (*dṛṣṭārtha*) taught therein are fruitful, it is inferred that the scripture as a whole—which concerns the unperceived (*adṛṣṭārtha*)—is likewise non-erroneous.

This has also been stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: [The text continues with the verse: "Since the fruits of the rites taught in this scripture are observed to be effective for those seeking worldly ends, therefore, by inference, the truth of the scripture regarding the supreme goal is established."
O bull among sages, it is through the threefold inference of specific characteristics, and through scripture arising from the speech of a reliable person, that certainty is attained; not otherwise.
And if that authoritative person is now examined as being established through scripture—
namely, from Ayurveda, from mathematics, and from the clear exposition of mantras— then [he is indeed proven].
"Because it is obtained through the elaborate teachings of the *Rasopaniṣad*, it is fully grasped.

Now, one might object: "The deity itself is not yet established; for only if that [deity] were established could there be the establishment of Īśvara as its specific form. But she is merely a word. To explain: the fruit arises solely from the performance of ritual action, not from the deity.

Because it is not established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the distinction of words such as "Rudra" or "Indra," which are intended to be subverters of that [notion]; for this very reason, since the apprehension of a relationship with that [word] is impossible, it is not established even by scripture (*āgama*). And precisely because the apprehension of the relationship depends on that [scripture], there is non-establishment due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Consequently, [in the case of the injunction] "the *caru* for Rudra..."

The followers of Jaimini maintain that in injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," that very word denoting the deity is understood as a constituent part of the qualified ritual act by virtue of being the objective factor (*uddeśya-kāraka*); therefore, it is logical that the fruit results from the action itself, not from the deity.
To this, it is replied: if the deity were thus merely a matter of words, then the fruit [would likewise be a mere word].

64) It would be nothing more than mere sound, because even the fruit consisting of heaven and so forth in such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" is established by other means of knowledge in exactly the same way. Now, if [it is argued that] from the word...
It is well-established in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other sources that no word whatsoever can exist without denoting an object;

therefore, it is said here that the specific word "heaven" (svarga) itself denotes a particular result. This being the case, the deity is not the word alone, but rather the specific object denoted by it, which is distinct from its own designator, such as Devadatta and so forth.

"Just like the self denoted by words," [it is argued]; however, that [word] alone bestows the fruit, whereas action alone—like the act of plowing and so forth—possesses the capacity merely for the production of a result. This is because, being insentient, it lacks the discrimination [to think], "I shall give this fruit to this person. For even you accept that a word is established as a communicator of meanings through its known words and word-meanings.

Since it is established that even words such as "Indra" convey their meaning solely by virtue of being words, the referent denoted by them—the deity characterized [as the object of worship]—is established just like the result characterized as heaven. Furthermore, the establishment of the deity characterized as Īśvara through inference and other means has already been stated; thus, it is not unestablished by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence (*itarāśraya*). As they say: "In order to establish the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), one must be diligent regarding what is perceived in the Veda; one should not practice laxity toward the specific effort required for the establishment of the Veda.
Consequently, [this applies] to a specific deity established by such Vedic revelation as "the Soma-drinker, the performer of a hundred sacrifices" (*somapāḥ śatakratuḥ*).

Since it is impossible for there to be a mere word established by scripture— such as "I praise Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand, who has a thousand eyes, and four arms"— for one whose nature is not determined by action, the deity qualified by those respective attributes is indeed established.
Scripture also [confirms] that deity through such specific qualifications.

65) It is observed, for example, in such passages as "Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over earth," and so forth. Nor should it be argued that because a deity possesses a physical form (*mūrtatva*), its presence at sacrifices performed in various locations—such as those involving people like ourselves—is impossible; for this [deity]...

Indeed, through the yoga of powers such as *aṇimā* (atomicity) and others, simultaneous presence in many places is entirely possible by the power of *prākāmya* (the ability to will reality), just as in the case of Vāsudeva’s possession of the *saubharya* (the celestial chariot). For it has been stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"When a mantra abides as mere sound, its fruit likewise consists of mere sound."
Nor is there a word devoid of meaning that possesses the sequential order found in phrases and sentences.
And the denoted object must be distinct from the denoter, just like the word "Devadatta" and so forth;
furthermore, according to you, the signifier would be devoid of the meaning conveyed by the word.
Therefore, that deity who is expressed is certainly distinct from the expressive word,
since there is a qualifier for her that denotes the form of the ritual action.
Because a deity, even when praised with such specific Vedic verses, becomes favorably disposed through that very praise, one should proceed with particular care using such Vedic utterances.
Now, if that qualification of the deity is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda),
then what contradiction could there be with ultimate reality?
It is heard in the scripture that from the deity alone comes great fruit;
because she is endowed with great power, he shall abide in her creation.
"Just as for the Vedāntins, infinity is a favor [to them], who is there that understands this meaning?
Who knows that words are devoid of meaning? Thus it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "The form of the deity is never like the body of those such as ourselves."
"Endowed with distinguished sovereignty, she is seated; this is not an illustration," and so forth.
If this were the case, then because Īśvara also possesses a body, he would—like ourselves and others—be non-omniscient and a non-universal creator.
It might be so; however, in that case, the status of being a supreme authority (paramāpta) would be untenable. If he were bodiless, his agency would be untenable, as they say:
"An effect is always pervaded by an agent endowed with a body."

"Because the world is an effect, it follows that its creator must be embodied. And: "For a controller who is bodiless would be like a liberated soul. Consequently, since the Lord (*īśvara*) would also be impermanent due to having parts, he too would require another creator; and for him as well, by virtue of being embodied...

If there were a dependence on another agent, it would lead to an infinite regress. Therefore, this is not the case, because we observe that the Self possesses agency through mere will in the movement of its own body and so forth, without depending on another body. Now, one might object: agency through mere will is observed in the case of the movement of a body presided over by oneself, but not in the case of external objects produced from clay and the like.

In the case of a jar and so forth, this is true; for this very reason, the universe is inferred to be like the body of the Lord, by virtue of his being its eternal substratum. Therefore, the Lord extends creation and other acts through mere will alone. For it is precisely due to their connection with impurity (*mala*) and the like that individual souls (*ātman*) require a body and senses for knowledge and action; however, for the Lord, [these are] eternal.

Because it is stainless, there is no dependence on that at all. As it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: "Just as time, though formless, is seen to bring about results, so too Śiva, though formless, accomplishes his work by means of his will."
And in the *Mohakārikās*:
"He who is untouched by the connection with impurity is omniscient, the all-doer, and all-pervading.
He is whole, partless, infinite, and the performer of endless effects according to His own will.
As for Śakti (Power), while performing the effects of the body, senses, and so forth, she is described as the "body" and the "instrument" of the Lord.
This has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra-tantra* and other scriptures:
Because the root and other [levels] are impossible, the body of the All-pervasive Lord is not of such a nature [as that of the individual];
rather, His body consists of five mantras which are employed for the fivefold cosmic acts.

"O Lord, [the limbs] beginning with the head are said to be formed by the faces Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha. Thus, Śakti, while performing the functions of the body, is designated by the terms 'body' despite the absence of a physical body. Furthermore, although her divisions are Vāmā and the others, they too are described by the wise according to the distinction of their functions. And the instrument is not other than Śakti; Śakti is not...

And by the passage beginning with "accumulated by volition" (*cetanācita*), its instrument is also seen in the Śruti; yet that [instrument] is seen to be neither identical with nor additional to it. For it is heard in scripture: "His supreme power is indeed manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action. Therefore, even this knowledge does not depend upon a body or sense organs. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"He who is omniscient [is so] because of his being the creator of all; it is well-established that whatever one knows, one performs, together with the means, the auxiliaries, and the fruits."
Because its own manifestation is devoid of activity, it does not depend upon a manifestor;
therefore, it is not subject to doubt, nor is it ever appropriate for it to be known erroneously.
Those [powers] which they seek to be manifested, because they are enveloped by the powers of impurity,
may indeed be obstructed in accordance with the requirements of the manifestor.
The stainless knowledge of Śiva shines eternally upon all objects, neither through direct perception, nor through inference, nor even through verbal testimony.
(68) [Objection:

How then is the body of Īśvara praised in the Āgamas with such expressions as "five-faced" and "three-five-eyed"? [Response: It is solely for the purpose of meditation (*dhyāna*). [Objection: That is not so; for meditation, worship, and the like are possible only when there is a form for meditation. As it has been said:
In the venerable Pauṣkara and other scriptures, this form is traditionally taught for the sake of the practitioner's goal:
"It has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides."
By such statements, others have also said:

"You possess form; therefore, You must necessarily be worshipped, for the intellect cannot grasp a reality that is formless. How, then, can there be the status of a teacher who imparts instruction in scripture? [This would be impossible] by mere will alone [if the Lord were formless], as in the case of the Vidyeśvaras and others.

In this context, being an "instructor" (*upadeśakatva*) consists precisely in making the scriptures understood, and not in the activity of the organ of speech. As it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "Because, when He is present, the accomplishment of every task is possible."
Even when the capacity is not impaired, it is observed in the self of that farmer.
"Likewise, the Lord's capacity for all actions is innate.
Others also say:
"By his mere presence, as if he were a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi)..."
"Instructions issue forth at will from walls and other such obstacles.

Therefore, this Śaiva Āgama possesses authority because it was composed by the Lord (Īśvara). Now, one might object: "Are not Hiraṇyagarbha and others also heard of as Lords in other philosophical systems?"

What is his distinction over them? To this it is replied: because they consist of the nature of *paśu* (the bound) and *pāśa* (the bond), they are preceded by another Lord; therefore, their status as the Lord of all is not possible. For instance, in other [texts], it is *prakṛti* itself that is denoted by the word Nārāyaṇa.

Furthermore, regarding that Īśvara who is postulated by certain knowers of the inner self (*adhyātmavid*) and by the Pāñcarātrikas—because he possesses the nature of being the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) and so forth, [he is not distinct] from Prakṛti... "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose. (RV 10.121.1)

On account of the meaning of such Vedic passages as "In the beginning, the one Lord of all that exists was born," the Lord known as Hiraṇyagarbha is proclaimed by the knowers of the Ātman as the Lord of that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) in its state of transformation; or, according to the divisions of the Pāñcarātra, He is characterized as the fourfold Self (*cāturātman*). As it has been said:

"Kṛṣṇa, Aniruddha, Makaradhvaja, and Rohiṇeya were the lords of the state of Prakṛti"— since these too possess birth and cessation, there must necessarily exist another creator for them, just as there is for Brahmā, Indra, and the rest. Furthermore, he who is the Lord by virtue of his connection with the intellect (buddhi)—

This has been stated by the Pātañjalas; however, for the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, that [soul] possesses lordship (*īśvaratva*) only through conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Since this conjunction is, by the very nature of being a conjunction—like the conjunction between a jar and a cloth—non-eternal and non-pervasive, lordship does not exist everywhere or at all times. Therefore...

Even among the lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvarāṇām*), there must be a giver; and since he who is thus the giver of all is precisely the one we accept as Maheśvara, his status as preceded by a giver is unestablished [for him]. Now, one might object:
how can this be so, given that the various lords established in other philosophical systems are themselves established by both worldly experience and the Vedas?

If it is argued that the status of Maheśvara is being rejected, that is not so; for the status of Maheśvara is demonstrated precisely through the conduct well-known in the world and through scriptures such as the Vedas. Thus says the Śruti:
"Rudra is indeed one, there is no second besides him. Here, by the restriction and the negation of a second, it is Rudra alone [who is meant].

The state of Maheśvara is established [as the goal]. Even among the Rudras, it is said in the Purāṇas: "Salutations again and again to Maheśvara, the blue-throated Tryambaka. Also in the Bhārata and other texts: "Neither by medicinal herbs, nor by mantras, nor by elixirs (rasāyana) is such well-being attained as that which comes from the chanting of Your name."
In the hymns composed by Vāsudeva, Arjuna, and others, such as the *Saptaśatarudrastotra*, he alone is renowned as Maheśvara. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhagavadgītā*:

In the tenth chapter, [the Lord] says, "Those who know Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds," thereby declaring that the Great Lordship (maheśvaratva) of the venerable Lord Nārāyaṇa pertains only to the seven worlds, beginning with Bhūḥ, and not to all the worlds and so forth. How then [is it that they] lie down?

It has been stated that the divine (*daiva*) is superior to Keśava. For this very reason, he is declared to be superior to the eightfold class of divine origins—ranging from Piśācas up to Pitāmaha—which pertains to the material creation; however, there is no contradiction in this, as he is not [declared] to be Maheśvara. As it is said: "The divine is of eight varieties, and the animal womb is fivefold."

"And the human [creation] is of one kind; thus, in brief, is the elemental creation. In this very same way, it should be understood regarding Candra, Brahmā, and others as well. As it has been said: "Agni is indeed the lowest among the gods, the offender.
Even in the world, [the status of] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others is established through their lordship by such titles as "Lord of the Discus" (Cakrasvāmin) and "Lord of Mathurā" (Madhurāsvāmin).

There is renown. Indeed, the Blessed One himself is renowned at Prayāga and other such places—his own respective fields—as Maheśvara, Sthāneśvara, Bhūteśvara, and so forth; and even at the sites of his consecration, he is renowned as Brahmeśvara, Someśvara, and others. Therefore, although he is recited [in the scriptures] in that way, it is nevertheless otherwise.

That state of equality is observed even in those who possess power, wealth, and so forth; furthermore, sovereignty in the form of lordship is established even in extremely fierce kings and others. Even by way of worldly renown, he alone is established as Maheśvara. And it has been stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "Īśvara is understood through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). It is not [otherwise].

And it is established by valid means of knowledge, as they say: "The word for substance, the word for genus, the word for action, and likewise another, the word for quality, the etymological (yaugika), and the conventional-etymological (yogarūḍha) are established solely through common usage."
The sun, a cow, motion, white, a lotus, and as with "a lotus"—
because they denote their respective objects, such a word is said to be "tadvidha" (of that kind).
Now, as for the objection that common usage (*prasiddhi*) is non-authoritative like the case of a yakṣa in a banyan tree, that too is incorrect.

For it has been stated that all connection between words and their referents is based upon common usage. If that [usage] were non-authoritative, the meaning of the Veda would remain unestablished; thus everything would be inconsistent. This is so both from the perspective of the scripture and from the perspective of the world. Therefore...

It has been stated by us in the *Pāṣaṇḍaparājaya* that Maheśvara is a perfected being (*siddha*): "She who is worshipped by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the words of the Purāṇas, by the foremost of sages, and by others..."
Having ascertained the sovereignty of the Moon-crested Lord,
how can human beings still be so utterly deluded?
In this world, from the highest beings, beginning with Brahmā, down to the smallest ants, by all classes of living creatures,
Giriśa’s lotus feet are worshipped.
"But no one else is to be worshipped by Giriśa.

Therefore, because it was revealed by the Supreme Lord—the omniscient, omnipotent, and supreme authority—the means of valid knowledge known as the Śaiva Āgama should be understood as being the most excellent of all. For this very reason:

There is no contingency of this [scripture] being rejected as unworthy of acceptance— unlike the Buddhist and other scriptures which contradict the Vedas that establish the system of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama)—
because its eligibility is restricted here to those situated within the castes and stages of life, because it does not contradict the Vedas, and because it is accepted by those who know the Vedas.
As it is stated in the venerable Parākhyatantra: "Initiation must also be performed for all those who are joined to the application of that [divine] power.
This applies to all three castes, but not to Śūdras, those of the lowest birth,
and so forth— provided, however, that those Śūdras who do not drink liquor are devoted to the practices and rituals of the Śaiva tradition.
"And that initiation must be performed for those who are devotees of Śiva, otherwise it is not [to be done].
Also, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:
"In whatever caste a person situated [in that state] has received initiation into the nature of Śiva..."
Remaining constantly established in that very state, one should protect the dharma of Śiva.
And it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅgendra* and other scriptures:
"Having performed the bath up to the head and having sipped water for purification,
one belonging to two stages of life (*dvirāśramī*) should worship the Sandhyā established by the Vedas, facing either north or east."

The successful accomplishment of the means for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) is known from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) alone; for it is rooted in that, as is the case with the *Smṛti* and other [texts]. Thus it is said: "Having first sipped water, the twice-born man should perform the Brāhmaṇic twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*)," and likewise: "One should not, even in thought, disregard the conduct prescribed for the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*); whoever [does so] in whichever stage..."
"Remaining established in that very [state] after having attained initiation whose essence is Śiva, one should also observe the dharma of Śiva.
Thus, in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other texts, the practice of great sages such as Śveta, Upamanyu, and others is heard of in this regard; and likewise in the Mahābhārata:

In the case of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as Aśvatthāman, it is said: "By these two, the Lord was worshipped in his linga-form; in every age, [the deity is worshipped] in that very image. Thus, in the Svarṇākṣa [Purāṇa], there is the attainment of success through the worship of the Supreme Lord Vāsudeva.
Furthermore, in the Rāmāyaṇa and in the hymns to Kārtavīrya and others, the dharma preceded by installation (pratiṣṭhā) is heard.
"One who properly constructs a temple of Śiva using baked bricks," and so forth—
as stated in the Sūtra— and "he shall point out liberation" in the Upaniṣads such as the Śvetāśvatara and the Atharvaśiras.

Furthermore, Śiva’s status as the one to be worshipped is heard in such passages as: "Having known Him who is subtler than the subtlest, the creator of the universe in its midst, possessing manifold forms, and the sole enveloper of Śiva—having known that Śiva, one attains absolute peace"; and "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, He who brings about auspiciousness; abandoning everything else," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not subject to contradiction, nor is its root severed, nor is it accepted by anyone [as false].
Therefore, it should be accepted as authoritative both by those learned in the Vedas and by others. As it is said in the *Mokṣakārikā*:
"And its object is not obstructed by any other means of valid cognition."
"Therefore, even those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) should accept that which is a means for attaining a result superior to that [of the Vedas].

Consequently, the Supreme Lord alone is the supreme authority (*paramāpta*). Kapila and others, however, are not supreme authorities because they propound mutually contradictory doctrines. As they have said:
If the Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not?
Furthermore, if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference of opinion between them?

And therefore, having first demonstrated the state attained through all other scriptures without contradiction, and because it reveals meanings not previously understood, it— like the Vedas and other general scriptures— accomplishes the fruits described therein according to one's qualification; thus, even though it is not their specific domain, it [reveals] the particular nature of enjoyment and liberation.

Furthermore, because it is the means for attaining the fruit, the authority known as the Śiva-āgama is unimpeded. As they say: "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which makes known an object not yet cognized. For this very reason, it was stated by the perfected masters (*siddha-guru*s):
"It is the accomplisher of all fruits without exception. As it has been said in the *Āgama* scriptures:
p.
74) "That which exists in the Śiva-āgama is not found elsewhere; that which is seen in the knowledge of Śiva does not exist anywhere else.
Therefore, in case of conflict with this [knowledge], those [other scriptures] are sublated. As for the sublation of that which is to be destroyed, it has been said:
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"At that time, the words of the Ṛṣis were not [accepted] by men; nor were the words of the gods [accepted] by the sages;
nor were the words of Brahmā [accepted] by the gods; nor were the words of Viṣṇu [accepted] by the lotus-born one."

"A Śaiva [teaching] is never sublated by the words of a Vaiṣṇava, nor is a Vaiṣṇava [teaching] ever sublated by a Śaiva. Also, in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*: "The Purāṇas are sublated by the Vedas, and the statements found therein are sublated by the Āgamas."
"The speech concerning Śiva is both general and specific, and indeed characterized by its particularity."
In the *Mokṣakārikās*, it is stated: "He is obstructed by those [afflictions] which are both specific and general;

for they are of a different nature from him, and likewise, because he is not their object. If this were so, other scriptures would not be authoritative. This is not the case; for others [the scriptures] are indeed authoritative within their own respective domains.

Although those respective authors lack omniscience, they possess knowledge and other qualities regarding their own specific subject matter; for this very reason, it was stated by them—who do not perceive all objects—that anything other than their own scripture is not authoritative. However, by Śiva, who perceives all objects, it has been declared that all [scriptures] are authoritative within their respective domains.

In the *Śrī-sarvajñānottara* and other such texts, it is stated that "the Buddhist, endowed with knowledge and conduct, shall attain the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*)," and so forth. They consider the attainment of these very principles to be the supreme liberation.
This is incorrect; for above those [principles], there remain karmas whose fruits are to be experienced in various worlds, as established by both reasoning and scripture.

And because the bonds of impurity (*mala*) and the rest have not been destroyed, and because there is a lack of thorough knowledge of the reality of Śiva and other [principles] which constitute the cause for attaining the supreme state (p.
it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
That which is isolation resulting from the discrimination between the Spirit and Primordial Matter; or that cessation which comes from realizing that all is Brahman;
or whatever other liberations arise from the severing of bonds—[all these are included here].
"All those various [powers] undergo differentiation in the process of emanation.
Thus it was said by the venerable Guru Avadhūta as well: "In your doctrine, even the liberations are accomplished through the realization of existence (*bhava*)."
"They do not fail their commitment, just as rains do not fail the waters.
Now, what are the places to be attained by those established in that scripture according to other philosophical systems?
To this it is said:
The Lokāyata, however, [is so called] because of its acceptance of such tenets as: "Earth, water, fire, and air—these are the four elements";
"the person (puruṣa) is the body characterized by consciousness"; and "consciousness is like the power of intoxication; perception alone is the valid means of knowledge," and so forth.

He considers that liberation is merely worldly happiness, distinct from the elements such as earth and so forth existing within the interior of the manifest cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), as they are directly perceived. As they say:
"One should live happily as long as one lives; there is nothing beyond the reach of death."
Once the body has been reduced to ashes, how can there be a return?

And so forth. These are called the proponents of the sentience of the elements (*bhūtacaitanika*). For them, knowledge whose object is the four elements is indeed valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the description of other things is merely error. Likewise, for other disputants as well, there is validity in describing the thing that is their own specific object. The description of the nature of one's own object—my...
76) Furthermore, the assertion that there is a change in its essential nature is nothing but an error.

On the other hand, certain proponents of the Self (ātmavādin) maintain that the person (*puruṣa*) is beginningless and is bound by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) through the stream of causes and effects.

Because there is no destruction of the connection with the body and senses for those residing in that state and so forth, they declare liberation to be merely the abiding in the path of the stars through a connection with an even more exalted body, resulting from the remaining karma after the cessation of the currently perceived suffering body.

Others, however—the Āgneyas, Sauras, Vaiṣṇavas, and so forth—assert that liberation is the attainment of equality with deities such as Agni and others; they claim that beyond that there is no further state to be attained. For them as well, it would merely be the attainment of those various worlds and deities within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); therefore, they too are simply perfected beings (bhūtasiddhas).

Others, however, such as the Kaulas, who consider violence, sexual intercourse, and the like alone to be the means for attaining the goals of human life, believe that liberation consists in the attainment of a specific state through the destruction of the material body—according to the analogy of the pot and the cloth. They too, in reality, are "accomplished beings" (bhūtasiddhas) because they are established in the states of Piśācas and other such spirits. Thus...
Furthermore, the followers of Jaimini, the Mīmāṃsakas, maintain that this world was never otherwise than it is now, nor does it have any creator;

rather, the selves are eternal, and they alone are the enjoyers of fruits such as heaven and hell through the very actions performed by themselves. And for them, [the authority rests on] Śruti and Smṛti...

They say that the attainment of the supreme goal results from the performance of the prescribed obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites. As it is said: "One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid transgression;
one who seeks liberation should not engage in those rites performed for specific desires (kāmya) or those that are prohibited (niṣiddha)."
Manu and others also say that the cause of the cosmic egg is this very Supreme Brahman, which is to be attained through knowledge and not from any other source, because no other possibility exists.
Therefore, the self-existent Lord, having become manifest, manifested this [universe].
"His power manifested as the great elements and so forth, dispelling darkness," and so on.
Furthermore, since these [elements] are also accepted as being produced within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) from the *sattva* and other qualities, they are produced from *prakṛti*.

The principles (tattvas) beginning with the qualities (guṇas) do not exist at all; they are all, in reality, established as mere designations (tanmātra), and thus they are discussed here. However, the proponents of the sentience of the senses (indriyacaitanika) assert that the senses themselves, distinct from the body, are what is denoted by the word "self" (ātman) and nothing else; these are called the "senses-established" (indriyasiddha). Furthermore, regarding the nature of the senses:

The mind alone is the cause of worldly activity, the self, and that very same thing is the supreme Brahman; from it the entire universe proceeds. They say that this alone is to be attained through knowledge. As they have said: "The mind itself, when afflicted by the defilements of passion and the like, is indeed saṃsāra."

"That very [self], when liberated from those [attributes], is designated as 'liberation' (mokṣa). These are the ones among the proponents of the consciousness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-caitanyavādins*) who hold that the mind (*manas*) is the conscious self. Furthermore, those who maintain that what is to be attained through knowledge is the "I-notion" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) itself, which is otherwise indefinable (*nirūpākhya*), are the proponents of the consciousness of the "I-maker" (*ahaṃkāra-caitanyavādins*). As for those...

Those who consider the wind called *prāṇa*, which is of the nature of the function of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), to be the self—they too are proponents of the ego (*ahaṃkāracaitanikāḥ*), and they are likewise established upon the ego alone.
As for the Buddhists, they are proponents of selflessness (*nairātmyavādinaḥ*) and are of four kinds; among them are the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas.

The two proponents of the existence of external objects (Bāhyārthasadbhāvavādins), having accepted the momentariness of all things, consider the continuum of cognition itself— consisting of mental modifications and characterized by determinative apprehension— to be the self. However, the Mahāyāna Mādhyamikas maintain that the continuum of cognition alone, which is empty of external objects, is the ultimate reality.

They say that this very [continuum] is the cause of saṃsāra due to its connection with the latencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions and so forth, but there is no other entity such as a *ātman* apart from it. Among these [schools], some [assert] a continuum of pure consciousness through knowledge and conduct.

They say that liberation is the cessation [of the mind]. However, those who advocate for the extinction of the lamp consider even the subsiding of that [mind] to be liberation; they are called the Buddhists (buddhicaitanikāḥ). The Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, on the other hand, maintain that the Supreme Lord is the creator of the world, while the atoms are its material cause, and these [atoms] are eternal.

They assert that selves are eternal and non-pervasive, and that knowledge arises for them only through the conjunction of the self with the mind for the sake of experiencing karma. In this regard, the Naiyāyikas maintain that liberation is simply the cessation of cognition and other qualities of the self, resulting from the knowledge of the sixteen categories.

The Vaiśeṣikas, however, hold that [liberation arises] from the knowledge of words and their referents; this is the distinction. As they say: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), tenet (*siddhānta*), the members of a syllogism (*avayava*), reasoning (*tarka*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), discussion (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)."

"From the knowledge of reality comes the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Furthermore, it is said that the knowledge of the similarities and differences among the six categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—is the cause of the supreme good. [The qualities are] cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, and effort.

Furthermore, even according to the ultimate view (paramārtha) of those who accept the eternity of the self, liberation is defined as the absolute non-existence of the nine qualities of the self— dharma, adharma, and the [seven] saṃskāras; yet because they also accept that the self is insentient,
they regard the eight qualities beginning with dharma as being nothing other than the intellect (buddhi), and thus these qualities are established solely within the intellect.

The Arhats, however, having accepted the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda), maintain that the self is the very principle of the qualities (guṇatattva) itself— which, according to the logic stated by Patañjali, "the functioning of the qualities is mobile"— and which is of such a nature as to be non-pervasive, limited by the body it occupies, and subject to transformation.
Thinking that [the self] is eternal because of the complete destruction of beginningless delusion and so forth, they are therefore said to have attained the perfection of the qualities (*guṇa*).

Others, however, hold that for the *puruṣas* there is indeed a beginningless primordial nature (*prakṛti*), as well as the connection with that nature and the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). And there is no such thing as an eternal intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) for that which is beginningless.

79) Therefore, destruction is logical; consequently, even in liberation, a relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed must be admitted for the Puruṣa and Prakṛti. And liberation occurs solely through the exhaustion of beginningless karma.
They say that she (Prakṛti), being pure, continuous, unsurpassed, unlimited, and of the nature of eternal bliss, becomes the object of enjoyment;

and they are called the Sattvabhujas (enjoyers of goodness). Furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhyas, the Puruṣas are distinct for each body, eternal, changeless, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), stainless, and of the nature of consciousness.

The pervasive [souls] are indifferent, yet joined with afflictions such as beginningless ignorance; likewise, *prakṛti* is one, consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, eternal, devoid of consciousness, all-pervasive, and the material cause of the entire universe.

And she (*prakṛti*), having transformed herself into the form of the arrangement of principles (*tattvas*) starting from the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with earth, [manifests] her own self...
Because it presents itself as an object of experience to the Puruṣas, that very [Prakṛti] constitutes their saṃsāra. However,

when among them there arises through knowledge concerning the manifest and the unmanifest a non-erroneous cognition of the existent (sattva), preceded by the discrimination between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, then she, her purpose having ceased with respect to him, desists from him.

They say that isolation (*kaivalya*) consists of a state in which the essential nature and other characteristics of the *guṇas* are no longer perceived. As they have stated: "Just as the activity of insentient milk is for the sake of the growth of the calf, so the activity of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is for the sake of the liberation of the Spirit (*puruṣa*)."

"Just as a dancer, having displayed herself before the audience, desists from her dance, so too does primordial nature (prakṛti), having manifested itself to the person (puruṣa), desist. And its partial manifestations are as follows: [text continues].

The Pātañjalas, having accepted what was previously stated and having declared that among persons there is a certain one who is described as being free from afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth and who provides the instruction of the treatise,
seek liberation through a semblance of the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*). As they say:
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions (*kleśa*).

The Lord (*īśvara*) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, and their latent impressions; He is the teacher even of the ancients, and so forth. Through their [the yogis'] knowledge and other means, there occurs the exhaustion of the karma to be experienced, which is comprised within the categories of the *guṇas* and *tattvas*.

Liberation (mokṣa) is precisely the attainment of the world situated above that [guṇatattva]. As it is stated in the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*: "Since there is no perception of karma to be experienced in the realm above the guṇatattva, even the liberation (kaivalya) of the Sāṃkhyas is not logical, because [karma] has not been exhausted."

And from the *Pāñcarātra*, it is established that there exists a supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*) called Nārāyaṇa, which is distinct from the [three] qualities (*guṇa*); from this arise all things, both sentient and insentient, either directly or through a succession.

Furthermore, for those individual souls (*jīva*), there is liberation through knowledge, not through the bondage of karma; and by the destruction of that [bondage] through knowledge and so forth, there is the cessation of *saṃsāra*.
They say that the dissolution of the cause into that Supreme Self, whose nature is the complete pacification of all differentiated effects, is the supreme good. As it has been said:
"That Blessed One, Vāsudeva, is the primordial nature (prakṛti) beyond the qualities (guṇas)."
"They say that the Unmanifest has become manifest, and there is nothing higher than this. Thus, from the Supreme Prakṛti,
there arose the Lords Kṛṣṇa, Aniruddha, Makaradhvaja, and Rohiṇeya.

Thus it is said. Therein, the perfected ones (*siddha*) of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) are described—those who have become transformations (*vikāra*) of that [Unmanifest], such as Kṛṣṇa and others, and those who accomplish its realization.
And for one established in the *guṇatattva*, there is residence in the world of Viṣṇu. As it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"The Akṛta, the Kṛta, the Raibhava, the Brāhma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Kaumāra, the Auma, and the Śraikaṇṭha."

"The worlds [are] eight within the qualities. These Sāṃkhya followers and others, due to their lack of full understanding of Māyā and Mahāmāyā, consider Prakṛti—which is indeed possessed of objects—to be the Supreme Prakṛti and the Supreme Void.
However, certain adherents of that same school, having accepted Prakṛti itself as the Supreme Brahman, regard it as its illusory transformation (*vivarta*).

The Vedāntins say that the world is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is characterized as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); having explained the emergence of individual selves (*jīvātman*) and the phenomenal universe (*prapañca*), they state that liberation (*mokṣa*) consists in the dissolution of those individual selves into the Supreme Self through self-knowledge and other means. However, the Māyāvādins...
Since Brahman alone— established by such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman; there is not here any diversity whatsoever"— is real,
while all other things consisting of duality have as their sole essence a construction of ignorance and are therefore unreal, so too are the individual selves (jīvātman).

Because it is erroneous due to being defiled by ignorance, even though its essence is the Supreme Self— the reality established by valid means of knowledge and proclaimed as such— the phenomenal world of duality, designated as the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and dream-experience,
[is sublated] through the arising of perfect knowledge, which uproots the causes of error that stand in opposition to it.

When all delusion has been cast aside, the realization of the Supreme Self remains established solely in its own essential nature for one who has awakened from sleep; the prior stream of the individual self (*jīvātman*) comes to an end. This indeed they call supreme liberation. Therefore, they remain established in the very reality of the Person (*puruṣatattva*). As it is heard in scripture:
(82) "The Buddhists are established in the principle of intellect (buddhi); the Ārhats are established in the qualities (guṇas);
the knowers of the Vedas are established in the Person (puruṣa); and the Pāñcarātrikas are established in the Unmanifest (avyakta)," and so forth.

But those who maintain that Brahman is Word (Śabdabrahmavādins) assert that the supreme Brahman, which is denoted by terms such as "Supreme Space" (Paravyoman), is nothing other than the creative power (kriyā-śakti) of the Self; from that alone arises the manifestation of the world in the form of words and their meanings, and they claim that liberation consists precisely in the dissolution [of this world] through the thorough knowledge of that [power]. They too, in the ultimate sense...

The Paurāṇikas, however, while remaining established in the very principle of the Puruṣa, accept—as the Sāṃkhyas do—the entire collection of principles beginning with Prakṛti, as well as the twenty-sixth principle, the Lord (Īśvara), who presides over Prakṛti and Puruṣa; they declare that the supreme liberation consists precisely in attaining the status of a Gaṇeśvara within His realm, characterized by *sālokya* and other forms of proximity. Regarding them:

In reality, because [the soul] is subject to being impelled and because it lacks full knowledge of the reality beyond that, there is no supreme liberation. As it is stated in the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*: "Equal to Gaṇendra and Agni, their desires remain unfulfilled," and so forth. Likewise, even those who maintain that liberation consists in attaining equality with Paramāditya and others [remain bound], within their respective worlds (*bhuvana*).

Thus, it is established by implication that they attain liberation in the form of *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and so forth. The Pāśupatas, however, not admitting the existence of impurity (*mala*) distinct from *māyā*, maintain that when all bonds are destroyed through initiation (*dīkṣā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and other means,
liberation consists in the transference of qualities such as omniscience from the Supreme Lord to the perfected being (*siddha*), which is identity with Him.

However, because they do not thoroughly understand impurity (*mala*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and thus lack its destruction, their state remains within the principle of *māyā* itself. As it is heard: "The Pāśupatas [abide] in *māyā*, while the Mahāvratas [abide] in *vidyā*. Thus it is with those specific [schools] set forth in the Śaiva Purāṇas and other texts.

Even for the Vaidika and the Āśupata, their abiding is in this very state. Some proponents of the doctrine of liberation through birth claim that, upon becoming a *siddha* through the grace of Śiva, omniscience and other qualities arise [de novo]. Others maintain that, through the penetration (*āveśa*) of the Supreme Lord, omniscience and other such qualities [arise] in the *siddha*.
They say, "It would be so. However, since even those [entities] possess impurity, they lack the manifestation of their own ultimate qualities;
therefore, they too would remain in that very state. And as for the Great Vows (mahāvrata)...

Like the Sāṃkhya school, they maintain that even in the state of bondage the self possesses no agency, and that upon liberation, the perfected ones (siddhas) possess only omniscience, while the status of being the creator of all belongs exclusively to the Supreme Lord. As it is said in the *Padayakṣiṇī*:

From the perfected state of Paramaśiva, there is the distinction that while others possess authority that has ceased with respect to specific [levels] but remains unceased with respect to others, the Siddha, moreover, possesses authority that has ceased entirely and in every respect in solitude; such is the difference. And when this is the case, they declare that the designation "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers only to the path ending at the level of Vidyā-tattva, and not to the attainment of other levels.

From the perspective of ultimate reality, that [view] belongs to those who dwell in mere conventional truth (*tattvavāsin*), because they do not admit that [the individual soul] is the agent of all; thus it has been said: "But those of great vows abide in knowledge alone. Others, however, while admitting that the perfected being (*siddha*) possesses omniscience, maintain that he is impelled by the Supreme Lord. Still others...

Those who maintain the doctrine of an eternally flowing Lord (pravāhanityeśvara) assert that the status of being the creator of all belongs indeed to that Lord, even though he is distinct [from the individual soul]. Since their position establishes that [the soul] is impelled by the Lord, it ultimately results in the reality of the Lord. Some proponents of the non-duality of Power (śaktyadvaitavādins), having accepted Power alone as the supreme cause, maintain that the world is its transformation (pariṇāma). They...

And like the proponents of Vedānta, they consider liberation to be merely absorption (*laya*) through knowledge and other means. Since they accept that Śakti is the material cause (*upādāna*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), they remain established in the principle of Kuṇḍalinī-Śakti.

Furthermore, by some, the *Ānanda-tantras*—which are accepted as means for achieving the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) by the Kaulas and others—are [regarded] by all, including the Matsyas and so forth.

Because it was composed according to one's own whims and is thus fruitless, there is no acceptance of it here within the Śaiva tradition. In the manner thus described, others as well—namely the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa [traditions]—[are likewise excluded].

Even the various subsidiary streams known as the *Gāruḍa* and *Bhūtatantra* possess authority within their own respective domains. Thus, having accepted the authority of all scriptures (*āgama*) within their own respective domains, one observes that Śiva and other such realities lie beyond their scope; consequently, [one looks toward] the liberations taught in those scriptures.

It has been stated that the very [scripture] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it demonstrates supreme liberation— which consists in the manifestation of one's true nature, which is characterized by non-return and equality with Paramaśiva, being more excellent than anything else. This validity of all the scriptures was established there by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha.
It is stated in the *Śrīmadrauravavṛttiviveka*:
"That which is called 'rejection' refers to those who, through mutual contradiction, claim that all scriptures suffer from sublation (*bādha*) and lack authority."
Those who abide [in the Śaiva path] and desire liberation as non-dual with that [Śakti] within the principle of Śakti;
and those who [desire it] within the principle of Vidyeśvara, [seeing] the Lord (Īśvara) himself as impelled by that [Vidyeśvara].
Those who [perceive] the Lord of Sages as omniscient within the purity of Mantra and Śuddhavidyā,
and those who perceive the Lord as one whose qualities have been transferred and whose own consciousness is lost within Māyā;

They remain; this is the distinction regarding liberation: this [state] is pure, while that which is produced by the vision of a bound soul (paśu) is not. Those who claim that Brahmanhood exists in the bound soul due to an impure transformation of consciousness (cid-vivarta) [are mistaken].
And in that very same [text]:
"That which was previously the manifestation of the power of action, the supreme Speech;
that which is unmanifest, the material cause of the qualities, and the Brahman of the selves."
In this very context is the means for those who are called Nārāyaṇas— those who,
by the power of the teaching on discernment, [perceive] man as distinct from the qualities upon the surface of the qualities.

Those men who, due to the cessation of qualities such as knowledge and so forth, are deluded in their intellect regarding the qualities that possess manifold aspects and function through the power of *syādvāda*.
Those who, through delusion, [assert that] in the modification of the intellect there is merely cognition that perishes in a moment;

But those who, through delusion, hold that the mere vital breath (prāṇamātra) resides within the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti), and that which exists in the mental faculty (manas) and the functions of the senses (indriyavṛtti) is merely a cause for another delusion; [they are mistaken].
Having understood that the senses themselves are the senses within the senses, those who know them as the Self,
and having reached the subtle elements, they declare that which has become Brahman to be the cause of the cosmic egg.

Those who have attained perfection through violence and sexual indulgence remain in the state of Piśācas and similar beings; likewise, those among the Bhūtas who, having acquired consciousness, know it to be composed of the elements.

I consider those who, having attained liberation through their own will, remain established in it because of another's vision, to be knowers of that reality who are joined with the respective principles; so it should be understood by the wise.
That with which the mind is endowed therein is called "possessed" by the wise;
having eternally attained this consciousness, they naturally pervade it themselves.
Even though it is maintained that there is something else to be attained beyond the principles (tattvas) on the right-hand path,
nevertheless, that very [state] is what is described, because of the singular determination toward the goal to be accomplished.

The distinction of that which is imperceptible is established through its effect; this distinction belongs either to the cause itself, or it is established as if already accomplished by virtue of being distinct from or non-distinct from the effect.
Since those [entities] are established by these effects, they are known through those other [effects];
they are indeed the principles (tattvas) by name, yet there is no difference between the name and the object.
Even in that case, although an element of error exists in them to some degree,
they nevertheless possess non-erroneous cognition by virtue of those inferences based on real effects.
Error, which consists in the superimposition of another object upon that which possesses real properties,
does not depart merely because its effect has ceased; therefore, it is not possible for anyone to destroy it.
Those by whom the sun-gem is perceived as the cause of fire—
even if through delusion— how could they not be deluded regarding that [fire] from the perspective of ultimate reality?
Therefore, although an object is imagined by them through their own volitions,
nevertheless, due to contradiction at the end, they enter into that very nature [of non-existence].
That which is abandoned for the sake of attaining those [qualities] is called their delusion;
because it is the adversary of that attainment, it is also an obstacle to attainment itself.
For this Self, which consists of the thirty-six principles and abides in a sequential order,
the attainment of even a single part of those principles is neither non-existent nor fruitless.
Thus, because the object to be attained remains undivided according to each individual scripture,
the validity of all scriptures has been declared by him on the basis of their non-contradiction.

"Thus, the validity of all scriptures was proclaimed by the Lord; and in some places, Rāmakaṇṭha, following that [teaching], has explained it through reasoning as established by the instruction of his teachers.
And the entire collection of treatises is divided fivefold according to distinctions such as the worldly (*laukika*) and so forth; among these, the worldly...

The *śāstra* consisting of Āyurveda, Daṇḍanīti, and so forth has visible results; that which is Vedic, such as Mīmāṃsā and the like, has both visible and invisible results; the spiritual (*ādhyātmika*) consists of Vedānta, Sāṃkhya, and so on, having the knowledge of the Self as its result;
furthermore, the *atimārga* such as Pāśupata and others has the attainment of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Māyā as its result; and the *māntra*...

That which is called Śaiva bestows the fruits of both supreme and lower enjoyment and liberation, as well as the instruction on the means thereto; therefore, in other scriptures, the thorough knowledge of Śiva and the others, as well as the nature of enjoyment and liberation and the exposition of their means,
are not clearly defined.
As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Because the author is all-seeing, the summary of the subject matter is not [stated] explicitly."
Just as those means are fruitful, so too in Śaivism all this is supreme.

Now, an objection is raised: since other currents—the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Gāruḍa, and Bhūta Tantras—are also well known as Śaiva, how can there be a difference in their essential subject matter? It is replied:
because they propound mutually contradictory doctrines, it is impossible for them to have a single author, just like the Sāṃkhya and other systems; therefore, [the author] must be omniscient.
Since it is impossible for Śiva— who benefits all and is free from passion, hatred, and the like— to express contradictory meanings,
there must be someone who, as in the case of Praṇava and others renowned as the bringers down of knowledge such as the *Kāmika* from the Supreme Lord,
is the bringer down of other currents (*srotas*) from Paramaśiva; this is stated in this scripture.
Furthermore, because they are not seen in the [original] scriptures, those [Tantras] were not composed by Paramaśiva; rather,

they were produced by other [scriptures] denoted by the term "Śiva," which are presided over by the Śakti of Tatpuruṣa-Śiva and favored by the varying degrees of the transformation of impurity (mala) and the respective qualifications [of the recipients], such as Vāmā and the others.

There is no contradiction in [describing them as] "excellent. And these are indeed valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to their own respective domains. As it is said in the *Ratnatraya*:
"The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) alone is the final conclusion; everything else is a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Śiva alone is the scripture (*āgama*); others are considered non-Śiva."
In the venerable *Mṛgendra* as well:
"The streams [of scriptures] are the Kāmika and others above; the Asitāṅga and others to the south;
the Sammoha and others to the north; and the extensive Tāla and other Tantras to the east."
And the first [is] Caṇḍāsiddhārā and so forth, under the protection of Caṇḍanātha.
Thus, how is it that in that very same [text] it is said:
"At the time of creation, Maheśāna, for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human beings,
bestows pure knowledge characterized by five streams"?

(p. 88) For this very reason— due to the instruction that it is "pure" (*vimala*), because it encompasses the five mantras, because it establishes the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*), and because it is manifested as the body of Śiva consisting of the five mantras— it is indeed of the nature of the Siddhānta.

It has been stated that knowledge is characterized by five currents (*srotas*). For this very reason, those situated within the other currents are universally renowned as Śaivas. As it is said in the venerable *Ṣaṭsahasrikālottara*:
"In the level beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*) is that called Kāmika; from the level of tranquility (*śānti*) indeed arises the Yoga of the All-pervasive Lord."
Know that it is inconceivable; from knowledge arises the foundation, which is of the nature of the cause.
The faces of Śiva are indeed named Ajita and Nivṛtti;
the heart of Śiva is Dīpta, and the head is likewise called Sūkṣma.
The crest of Śambhu consists of a thousand [rays]; from Aṃśumat comes the armor;
the eye should be known as Suprabha, resembling the moon, the sun, and fire.
From his crown was born the Vijaya-tantra, from his forehead the Pārameśvara,
and from his eyes the Niśvāsa emerged in three sections in ancient times.
The two-portioned Udgītha, sung forth by the two ears for the sake of enjoyment and liberation,
should be known as the thirtyfold reflection of the face, emerging from the mouth.
Likewise, the Saiddha is three hundred [units] long; the Grīvā arises from both of those;
and the Saṃtāna, measuring two kāṇḍas, extends out from the region of the palate.
The single division, Nārasiṃha, has emerged from the region of the chest;
and from the two breasts, that which is called Candrahāsa has emerged through their differentiation.
From the heart and the throat, that which is called Vīrabhadra has emerged;
it is to be known as the Āgneya [Tantra] from the Vātula, and as the Ekabhedaka from the Jaṭhara.
From the navel region of Svāyambhuva, it spread forth by a single division;
from the body of Śiva, it arose as a twofold expansion on both sides.
From the region of Brahmā, Raurava is established as a single division;
from the waist, Prākuṭa arose, and that consists of three divisions, O Śāṅkarī.
The single division, however, is the *kiraṇa*, which has emerged from procreation; the *lalita* and the *siddhānta* are born from its various subdivisions.
"And the two-fold [knowledge] of the bull [Saurabheya] from the knees of Parameṣṭhin.
Therefore, by the statement that the scripture called Siddhānta is the most excellent of all, all knowable entities are established.
For here, Paśupati teaches that the three categories known as Paśu, Pāśa, and Pati are primarily to be known;

for all other [categories] are included within these very ones. As it is said in the venerable Mṛgendra: "The Lord of the World [revealed] the Great Tantra, which consists of three categories and four feet."

"Having summarized it by means of a single aphorism (sūtra), he speaks again in detail. In that regard, within the category of the Lord (pati-padārtha), there are the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, Mantramahēśvaras, liberated souls (muktātman), Śaktis, and Śivas,
as well as the collection of means for enjoyment and liberation, such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth, which are denoted by the [subsequent] sections beginning with "Action" (kriyā).
The summary: Within the category of the bound soul (*paśu*), there is a summary of the *vijñānākala*, *pralayākala*, and *sakala* [types of souls], as well as their subdivisions.

Regarding the category of the bound soul, however, the fetters (*pāśa*)—consisting of the power of obscuration (*malatirodhāna-śakti*), karma, *māyā*, and *mahāmāyā*—are summarized. This is also stated in the venerable *Mataṅga-tantra* and other scriptures.

90) Different designations and different enumerations of categories are heard [in various scriptures]. Even in those cases, there is no contradiction, because these same entities are expressed by means of different modes of presentation. Furthermore, the characteristics of Paśupati and the fetters (pāśa) have been explained.
In the venerable Parākhyatantra and other scriptures,

it is stated: "The Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the creator of all, the powerful, the knower of all, whose limbs are the mantras, who exerts himself in bestowing grace, who is peaceful, the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), and the awakener," and so forth.

"The individual soul (paśu) is distinct from the body, perishable, all-pervasive, differentiated, impure, insentient, the enjoyer of the fruits of its own actions, the agent, possessing limited knowledge, and dependent upon a Lord," and so forth.
Likewise: "The two powers of the Lord are *prāvṛti* and *īśa*; [the former consists of] karma and māyā, and their effect is fourfold."

"The net of bonds is, in brief, proclaimed by the very name of *dharmas*," and so forth. There are three kinds of bound souls (*paśus*): therein, the *vijñānākala* is endowed with *mala* alone; the *pralayākala* is endowed with *mala* and *karman*;

and the *sakala* is endowed with *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*. Furthermore, *mala* consists of the one [entity] that veils the self-knowledge (*ātma-vidyā*), and it is joined with manifold powers (*śakti*) that conceal knowledge.

[The Self] is eternal and all-pervasive. Karma also is distinct for each individual, characterized by a beginningless stream, having the self as its agent, and bestowing pleasure, pain, and so forth. Māyā is both pure and impure. Among these, the impure [Māyā] consists of the thirty principles beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth, along with the worlds contained therein, the elements, and the various states of existence.

Rodha-śakti, however, is the ultimate cause, eternal, pervading its own effects, and consisting of the true nature of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Śakti-tattva, as well as the worlds (bhuvanas) and so forth; she is the material cause of sound and, prior to the ripening of impurity (mala), performs for the sake of that ripening the function of concealment (tirodhāna) for bound souls (paśus) by way of metaphorical designation.

It is called a "bond" (pāśa). Furthermore, although Mahāmāyā constitutes a secondary liberation (aparamukti) for the attainment of the worlds, because those who have attained it remain subject to dependence and other such conditions relative to supreme liberation (paramukti), the three bonds are said to constitute bondage.
And this [is stated on page 91].
Since everything has been established in detail within the treatises (*śāstra*), it is not elaborated upon here. [Objection:
But sound (*śabda*) is indeed eternal; how then is Mahāmāyā said here to be established as its material cause (*upādāna*)? [Response:
It is said in reply that since phonemes (*varṇa*) are insentient and manifold, Mahāmāyā, known as *vidyā*, exists as their cause.
This is established. As it has been stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra* and other scriptures:
"Therefore, the *bindu* is the material cause (*upādāna*), for without it there would be no phonemes;
and since they are remembered as being of great number, they are produced through the activity of consciousness."
"For them, Īśvara is the efficient cause (nimitta), and that Bindu is the material cause (upādāna). Thus [it is said].

He now states the distinction of the *parabindu*, the supreme cause, which consists of the syllable *Amen*. Consequently, the Supreme Lord, from the supreme cause called *bindu*, sequentially produces the letters denoted by the term *mātṛkā*—beginning with words and so forth—as He is the cause of all sound, starting with *nāda*. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"From Śakti arises Nāda, then Bindu, then the Imperishable (Akṣara), and from that the Mātṛkā.
Now, it is observed that letters, which perish as soon as they are uttered, arise from the contact of the palate, lips, and other articulators.
And it is said:
"Sound, originating from space and air, issues forth from the body and enters the vocal tract;
being differentiated in various locations, that which attains the state of phonemes is called 'speech' (śabda)."

Thus [it is asked]: how can the *mātṛkā* be said to be born from the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*)?
