To this we reply: At the beginning of creation, the Supreme Lord produced the *mātṛkā-mantra* and the Siddhānta scripture consisting of mantra through the sequence beginning with *nāda*. And that is called "pure sound" (*śuddha-śabda*). As it has been said:
In the *Śrīmatparākhyatantra* and other scriptures, it is stated:

"The Bindu is pure; from its will, the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) arose," and so forth. And the *nādas* produced from that [Bindu], like other principles (*tattva*), serve as the conveyors of meaning for each individual person by the will of Śiva.
They are joined together. Furthermore, the accomplishment of *nāda* (sound) is to be observed in the *Nādakārikās*. As it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara* (p.
"That supreme seed called *nāda* resides within all beings."

And those sounds (nādas), existing within the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) and others, become the causes for the utterance of pure sound through the cooperation of the pure body of bindu and so forth. However, existing within bound souls who possess all [karmic limitations], they produce meaning through the differentiation of the utterance of sound by means of the sequence of the supreme syllable, bindu, and so on, in cooperation with the instruments and effects of māyā.
They also become the causes for spiritual practice; however, the sound uttered by them is said to be impure because it is produced from the illusory space and other elements.

Consequently, in the case of the sounds uttered by people such as ourselves—which resemble pure phonemes but are actually like embers—these [pure phonemes] are manifested through the medium of *nāda* by the will of the Supreme Lord and others, via His attentive intervention.

The pure phonemes, which occupy the position of fire, become the causes of the fruit. For this very reason, there is a distinction of the King of Mantras from words such as "jar" (ghaṭa). And it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "O Great Sage, that which is well-established in the distinction between the signified and the signifier..."
Among those [phonemes] which are employed or intended to be expressed according to the speaker's desire,
the phonemes are designated as "expressors" (*vācaka*) in the scripture concerning the arising of Śiva. Since the world is not independent, the Supreme Lord is independent.
The words uttered by practitioners are always present [to them];
yet, due to the insentience of persons, even the phonemes possess formlessness.
And I consider that, because the practitioner is dependent [on others] within the teaching,
the words "manas" and "sāṃnidhyatā" are established there through the penetration of power (śaktyāveśa).
Therefore, this position— that because the collection of word-meanings is eternal, the word itself is also eternal— is also refuted;
for the relationship between the signifier and the signified is created by the convention of the Supreme Lord,
and since it is impossible for one person to establish the convention for all words, [the meaning] must be understood as having unlimited power.
Because it has been stated that [this] belongs to the Supreme Lord. As it is said in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "Therefore, this [universe] is created by His will, devoid of sequential order."
Even the conventional sign was created by her and made known to people by her will,
because the world is not independent, being shrouded in the darkness of the fetters of karma.
Since every movement occurring therein is produced by that [agent],
therefore the creator of the convention stands as the cause of the entire lineage.
"The conventions of the mantras were likewise conceptualized by him alone; therein are many perfected [mantras] designated by the words of the Mātṛkā.
Thus it is stated in the *Mantravārttika* as well.
"Since Śambhu, the Lord of Vidya and Avidyā, created the mantras through both general and specific arrangements,
he is seen as the author of this designation, 'Arya' (the Noble One). Therefore,
because the composition of other words in the production of effects belonging to Māyā is performed by bound souls (paśus), [it is not the work of the Lord].

Furthermore, because even other streams [of thought] were composed by another Self, it is established that the scripture known as the Siddhānta alone is the most excellent. The activities of its author, the Supreme Lord, are fivefold, beginning with the subtle [creation].
As it is said in the venerable Mṛgendra: "The creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment..."

The liberations, the function, and the fruit along with its agent— this indeed should be known as belonging to Him alone. In that regard, the direct creation of Śiva proceeds from the material cause called *bindu*, preceded by the destruction of the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*),
and consists of the generation of bodies and so forth for the Vidyās, Vidyeśvaras, and others through the *bindu*, followed by the sequential production of sound.

And from the gateway of Ananta and others, through the material cause known as Māyā, there first occurs the production of the impure principles (tattvas), worlds (bhuvanas), and so forth, followed by the conjunction of the Mantreśvaras and the Sakalas with the effects and instruments belonging to Māyā. As it is said in the venerable Kiraṇatantra:
p.

94) "In the pure resonance (dhvani), Śiva is said to be the agent; in that which rests upon Ananta, the Lord [is the agent]. Thus, the maintenance of the entire universe—which has been restrained by His own will—is [effected] through its own activities.

Establishment is the fixing [of souls] in their respective states. Withdrawal, moreover, is the dissolution of both the pure and the impure, occurring in the reverse order of creation, namely the dissolution of Māyā and Mahāmāyā. Concealment consists in the experiencing of enjoyments by the selves according to their merit. Grace, however, is the severing of bonds and the manifestation of Śiva-nature.

And thereafter, the Supreme Lord, having matured the impurity of souls through the processes of creation and so forth, effects their liberation by means of grace. As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "Now, for the sake of bringing about the cessation of the bondage of the self, the continuity [of suffering], and the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*)."
And for the manifestation of the state of Śiva, the sixfold [path] is proclaimed here.
The path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) consisting of worlds,
the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), and the path of kalās (kalādhvan)— all these enter into the single state of Śiva.

And each of these is called a "path" (*adhvan*) because they are, respectively, the causes for attaining the state of Śiva. Among them, the *kalādhvan* consists of the five *kalās*: Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti.
The *varṇādhvan* consists of the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā, beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. The *padādhvan*...
Furthermore, the pervasive form of the sky consists of its constituent parts (*padāni*), which in some cases number eighty-one and in others sixty-six. As for the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*),

in some instances it consists of the mantras of Brahmā and Śiva along with the limbs (*aṅga*) excluding the two eyes, while in other instances it takes the form of the ninefold array (*navavyūha*) mantras and the mantras beginning with Śiva.
They differ according to each individual tantra. Consequently, a difference in mantras and a difference in ritual actions are the causes of contradiction between tantras.
Regarding this very point of differentiation, as stated in the sūtras of Bodhāyana and others:
"Since it is traditionally taught that a difference in tantra arises from the distinction between differences in ritual action and so forth."
Therefore, in that case, one should act exactly as it has been stated, and not according to another tantra—
whether [the procedure] is obtained through the power of the words or through the power of the meaning.
"By the power of the thing itself, that statement is obtained as it is from another *saṃhitā*.

Also, in the *Yājñasūtra*: "He who, transgressing his own *sūtra*, proceeds according to another *sūtra*, having rendered the *ṛṣi* [who composed his own] invalid, he too is joined with unrighteousness (*adharma*)."

The worlds (*bhuvana*) are the pure and impure abodes of experience. They are heard of in various enumerations according to each individual system (*tantra*). In that regard, there is no contradiction, as it is accepted that some [worlds] are included within certain others.
However, the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) is written here in detail for the purpose of demonstrating the gradations of the aforementioned abodes of liberation.

And that [creation] is of two kinds: impure and pure. Among these, the creation of the impure path is threefold, consisting of common, uncommon, and both. Therein, the uncommon creation is restricted to each individual soul and consists of the subtle body; the common creation consists of the worlds and so forth.

But that which consists of both forms is the nature of the body born of the world (*bhuvanaja*). Among these, it has been stated that the *māyā-tattva* is the supreme cause of the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*). From that [māyā] arise the principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*kṣiti*). From that [māyā], through *kāla*, *kala*, *rāga*, and *vidyā*, the manifest [evolutes] arise; from the *guṇas* comes the intellect (*dhi*); from the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) comes the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), as well as the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs (*indriya*).

"And from the *tanmātras* he created the gross elements and everything else in succession. Regarding this, the Commentator has stated that by the word "kalā," *niyati* (the principle of necessity) is also included through the method of *tantra* (multiple application). This is because *niyati* is heard of everywhere as being present there, just like the others. And it is said in that very same [text] concerning the path: "Below Māyā, however, the *kalā*-tattva is situated."

In the two [lower] levels there is Niyati, and in the other, the higher one, Kāla and Vidya; thus it is said again. Therein, according to the order of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), the five great elements beginning with earth [are situated]. This has been stated in the *Śrīmanmṛgendra* (p. 96) according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama):
Space, air, fire, water, and earth constitute the five elements;
they possess one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively, beginning with space and having the functions of providing room and so forth.
Their respective substrata are the five *tanmātras*. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—this pentad consists of *tanmātras* characterized by their qualities; they are so designated because of their connection with the term *tanmātra*."
And in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "The cause of that [gross element] possesses qualities identical to it and serves as its filler;
for this is the distinction of the subtle element (*tanmātra*) from the gross element—that [the former] is devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).
These exist as the substrata of the senses in both gross and subtle forms. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The subtle elements (tanmātras) here are like a paste for the great elements (mahābhūtas). Also, in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
"This effect, having entered through the instruments (karaṇas), is made to perform activity;
but because they are not all-pervading, the instruments exert themselves by presiding over the effect."
And those instruments (*karaṇa*) are divided into the organs of action (*karmendriya*), the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Among these, the five organs of action—known as the genitals, anus, feet, hands, and speech—are established as the instruments for performing actions such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, according to the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal taught in the venerable *Mataṅga*. And it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"Speech, hands, the organ of generation, the anus, and the feet—these arise from *rajas*. [Their functions are] speaking, grasping, walking, excretion, and movement," according to the statement. Furthermore, the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) are established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perception of smell and the other objects. As it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
The ear, the sense of touch, sight, the tongue, and the nose are the instruments of cognition;
the function of each of these is the preliminary observation (*ālocana*) of sound and the other respective objects.
The external organs are tenfold, consisting of the functions of will (*icchā*), exertion (*saṃrambha*), and cognition (*bodha*).
The internal organ is threefold, to be designated as mind (*citta*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*).

Therefore, the triad of internal organs—known as mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—is established therein; among these, the function of the mind is determined to be attention (*avadhāna*). And it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"It is the impeller of the senses, moving swiftly, and characterized by volition (*saṃkalpa*)."
"The mind consists of the auditory and other senses which grasp objects such as sound.
As for the ego (ahaṃkāra), it is the cause of the "I-notion" through its function of agitation (*saṃrambha*). This is stated in the *Bhogakārikās*:
"Agitation is the function of the activity of the 'I'. It is also said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Then, from the Manifest (vyakta), there arose the Ego (garva) of the intellect (buddhi), embellished by its instruments;

through its activity, the five bodily winds (vāyus) exert themselves. Furthermore, the fact that it is the cause of the notion of "I" (ahaṃ-pratyaya) has been established in detail in the venerable *Mataṅga*. And that is the Ego (ahaṃkāra).

Due to the predominance of the qualities of *sattva* and the others, it is divided into three types known as *taijasa*, *vaikārika*, and *bhūtādi*. Among these, from the *sāttvika-taijasa* [aspect], there arises the origin of the organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*)—which are illuminating—and of the mind (*manas*).
From the *rājasa-vaikārika* [aspect], there arise the organs of action (*karmendriya*), which are the causes of activity. And from the *tāmasa* [aspect]...
It should be understood that [this applies] from the *bhūtādi* [ego] to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). As it is stated in the *Bhogakārikās*:
"Since that group consisting of mind, intellect, and the deities is illuminating, it is born from the *sāttvika* ego, which corresponds to its own nature."
From the king’s own transformation, however, there arises a group of agents for the organs of action;
by means of this, the effect here conforms to its cause.

"From the ego (ahaṃkāra), the group of eight [is produced]; distinct from these two groups is the *prakāśya* (the manifestable), which is *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness), arising from that which is designated as *jātībhūta* and so forth. (p. 98)
Cognition (*buddhi*) is established as being the material cause of that [ego] and as the cause for the determination of external objects;
and it is produced from the principle of the *guṇas*. As it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
"From the *guṇas* previously agitated, there suddenly arises [cognition], which has the elements as its object."
Intellect, through its function of determination, is the auspicious mother of all things.

Furthermore, since dharma and the other qualities would have to be accepted as attributes of that [Self] by virtue of being its formative factors (saṃskāraka), it would follow that the Self is subject to modification. Moreover, since actions such as agriculture are observed to be formative factors of *prakṛti* alone, it is *buddhi* itself—endowed with the eight qualities beginning with dharma—that is described here. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Existence, intellect, the qualities, dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and prosperity—these are *sāttvika* when they are present; by their reversal, excluding passion (*rāga*), they are *tāmasa*."

And in the *Bhogakārikās*: "Non-dharma and the other three, passion (*rāga*), and dharma and the other four— consisting of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*— are the form of those born from their respective actions."

The *guṇatattva* is established through the three forms of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which are characterized by the qualities known as illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and restraint (*niyama*). As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Therefore, the secondary *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the material causes of the intellect and the other faculties."
Their functions, such as illumination and so forth, are indeed well known for the most part.
Although there are three secondary [categories], they are nonetheless a single reality because of their inseparability;
the singular designation for each of these is based on the predominance of its specific function.

And therefore, since the qualities (*guṇas*) are insentient and manifold, this *prakṛti* is established as unmanifest (*avyakta*), being the cause of those [qualities] and, as the substrate of the qualities, the material cause of the worlds such as Krodheśa and others. Thus it has been said:
In the *Śrīparākhyatantra* it is said:
"Because Prakṛti is the cause of the guṇas, the state of being an effect belongs certainly to the guṇas;
for by them, their own effects are established as distinct from the perspective of their being effects."

In this context, because the person (puruṣa) conjoined with the fivefold sheath beginning with *kalā* possesses manhood only in a figurative sense, and because that [manhood] is subject to dissolution, the Puruṣa is taught in the scriptures as the object to be purified (*śodhya*) for the sake of its purification during initiation. He is described as transcending the entire path (*adhvan*), just like Śiva, the purifier (*śodhaka*). However, because he is conscious, all-pervasive, and immutable, [he is not subject to change].

Because it is impossible for it to be the material cause of another principle (*tattva*) and because it lacks the status of being a support for the worlds (*bhuvana*), it does not have the nature of a path (*adhvan*). Therefore, the *puruṣa-tattva*, which consists of the application of the connection with the five coverings (*kañcuka*) and is characterized by the authority over experience (*bhoga-adhikāra*), is said here to be produced from *māyā*. This has been stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
Now, regarding the instruction on the principle of the individual soul (puṃstattva) as it approaches the self-sovereignty (svādhiṣṭhāna):
O tiger among sages, there is no second principle called "puruṣa" [other than this].
Pierced by the three sheaths and gradually seized by Time,
they fall and are embraced [by it] as they proceed toward the state of manhood, following their own course.

Thus, she who was spoken of as abiding in the differentiation of the reality of that Self—she, whose nature has been established, has been described by me to you exactly as she is, [who] will ordain the world and the seat of enjoyments within the All-pervasive One. Now, it may be objected that even in certain scriptures, worlds are heard of in relation to the principle of the Puruṣa. True; [they belong] to those who are its presiding lords.

The worlds are indeed heard of as being the locus of the Rudras; however, because the Puruṣa is conscious, he cannot be the support of the worlds, due to his connection with the impurity of manhood (puṃstva-mala).

They remain situated precisely within the state of being colored by the same location. For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "From that [Prakṛti] alone arose the principle of the Person (puruṣatattva), which is the basis for the cognition of the person; it is the fulfiller of Pradhāna and the rest, and it has its locus in Rudra within the world of Bhuvana. And in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"These Rudras, fierce with intense power, abide in the principle of *rāga* (attachment).
In that very place, the *puruṣa* is to be known as the guardian of the house of *pradhāna*.
Thus, *rāga* is established as that which generates desire in the self (*ātman*), whose knowledge and action have been perfected by *kalā* and *vidyā*.
As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"Even one who has perceived an object, if his power of vision has not been manifested [by initiation] and remains unattended, does not develop attachment toward that which produced it; therefore, the Lord created [the world] from that very [power]. And in the *Bhogakārikās*:
"Having attained the experience of objects of enjoyment, attachment toward that enjoyment arises;
for the sake of accomplishing that, there is passion (rāga) which colors one toward enjoyments.
Now, [this occurs] with respect to both proximate and non-proximate objects of the internal and external organs.

Because it is useful as that which presents objects to the senses, and because the intellect—having determined its object—is directly the object of experience, knowledge (*vidyā*) must be understood as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the Puruṣa in the act of grasping that [intellect]. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Thus, one who desires to see the range of the eye through the manifest power of action..."
He himself, being unable to see [the truth], has a need for favor from you.
For that purpose, the Lord, having agitated *kalā* alone which is capable of producing [the world],
created the principle called *vidyā*, the instrument of the Supreme Self.
"By means of that luminous form which promotes the power of knowledge, [the subject] cognizes the supreme object to be accomplished by all the causal factors. (p. 101)
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha* as well:
"Consciousness, which consists of the forms of objects and takes the nature of pleasure and so forth, is in brief the object of enjoyment;
even if it were of the nature of light like the sun, it would still [be an object] because of its status as an action."
"Dependent upon other causes, [the power] is capable of making itself manifest.

Furthermore, this triad of principles known as Unmanifest (avyakta), Attachment (rāga), and Knowledge (vidyā) was born from the principle of Limited Agency (kalā). As it is stated in the venerable Raurava:
"From the principle of Kalā, the two principles of Rāga and Vidya came into being."

And regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*): likewise, in the state of *pralaya-kevala*, because the person (*puṃs*) is shrouded by impurity (*mala*), even limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) is impossible; therefore, one should understand that *kalā* arises from the *māyā-tattva* for the purpose of removing a portion of that impurity. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

The agentive power of the individual soul is eternal and all-pervasive, like the power of the Lord; yet, being obscured by the ego, it does not shine forth among objects unless it is accompanied by grace.
Hara, having agitated Māyā, creates that supreme reality called Kalā, which is luminous (taijasa) and serves as the instrument for activity; for it is indeed the benefactor of that [limited soul].
"By that [consciousness], which is like a lamp, the atom of pure consciousness illuminates one part [of itself] after tearing asunder the dense darkness. Thus it is said;
and in the venerable *Mataṅga* as well:
"That which is extremely subtle and stainless, consisting of the nature of knowledge and action,
is cast down into worldly enjoyments by means of its empowered aspect.
Furthermore, because the Self is omnipresent and thus present everywhere, it belongs to all.

*Niyati* (destiny) is established as that which regulates the experience of the fruits of one's own actions, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of all karmic fruits occurring simultaneously. Furthermore, even for one whose enjoyment has already commenced, there is a dependence upon a limit; therefore, *niyati* is that which delimits [the experience] by means of duration such as "long" or "quick.
Time is established as having cognition as its characteristic; and it has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra* that both of these arise simultaneously from Māyā:
"The object of cognition, such as satisfaction and so forth, is time, which originates from Māyā."
"Perceiving the bound soul (paśu) as undetermined by necessity, from its very non-arising," thus [it is said].
Also in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "Now, Time (kāla), having arrived in due order, is seen through the three coverings."
"By which that subtle [self] is conceptualized through its connection with the power of Śiva. Thus [it is said].

Likewise, it is stated that "power (śakti) is the regulator of the person, together with the principle of necessity (niyati)," and so forth. Here, in the *Śrīman-mṛgendra* and other texts, Kāla and Niyati are listed below the principle of attachment (rāga) according to the order of their manifestation;
however, in the *Śrīmat-svāyambhuva* and others, they are listed according to the order of their origination. Thus, there is no contradiction.
This subtle body, consisting of the thirty principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *kṣiti*, is determined for each individual soul;
thus it is called the "common creation. And it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Beginning with *prayoktrī* and ending with the earth, this [subtle body] accomplishes its various purposes."
"It is also determined by the differences in individual experience.
Thus it is stated. Also in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
"This group of principles, beginning with the earth and ending with *kalā*, is restricted to each individual and wanders about under the influence of karma."

"And this [principle] exists in all bodies born of the world. Regarding this, some—like the Sāṃkhyas—accepting the identity of *prakṛti* and the *guṇas*, include *puruṣa* among the categories (*tattvas*) and thus state that their number is thirty.
That is incorrect, because it contradicts the aforementioned root scripture. And thus:
Therefore, the Māyā-tattva is heard of as the supreme cause of all the impure principles, eternal, pervasive of its own effects, and insentient; as it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"That one seed of the world is non-auspicious (aśiva) and possesses manifold powers."

By which causal property (hetu), characterized by being dependent on auxiliary factors, limited in scope, obstructed by its own end, pervasive, and perishable, is the agent inferred? This is the characteristic of the world (jagaddharma).
Therefore, there is also no grasping (upādāna) without the other [factors], such as the threads.

And here, because Māyā is eternal, it is impossible for it to be the substratum of the worlds and so forth; thus, those worlds reside only at the summit of Kalā. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Even in the *Māyā* [tattva], Gahaneśa and the other presiding deities are recited;
and the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*) occurs during initiation (*dīkṣā*), all of which is at the beginning of that [work].
And here, during initiation, [the purification] of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), which extends from the *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*), [ends] within the *prakṛti-tattva*.
Having severed the mere bestowal of worldly enjoyments and having established only the bestowal of enjoyments for the body existing above the *kalā*-tattva, a total severance must be effected;
this is called "immediate liberation" (*sadyonirvāṇa*). Presiding over that, Śiva himself becomes truly Śiva in the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*).
That [stream] must be severed; likewise, above the principle of Māyā (māyā-tattva), the impurity (mala) must also be severed.
In this way, there are many streams of the principle of Māyā. As it was said by Bṛhaspatipāda:
"Even the words of all the Siddhas would be exhausted if uttered for a long time; because of the infinity [of these streams] within Māyā, they cannot be fully described."

Regarding the "number of currents" (*srotasām saṃkhyā*): it is stated in the *Śrīmanmataṅga*—“[The channels] are shaped like honeycombs and filled with atoms. As for the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), it is indeed of a single form.
Thus, the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) has been shown. Now, the pure path is being demonstrated. In that regard, within which *tattva*...
The abode of the mantras numbering seventy million is the *vidyātattva*;
above that is the *īśvaratattva*, in which the lords of knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*) such as Ananta and others reside.
This has been stated in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:
p.
104) Having described the *vidyā-tattva* with the words "above that, however, there is another, the *vidyā-tattva*, O Six-faced One," and so forth, [it continues]:
"Above *vidyā*, however, there is another, the enclosure of Viśveśa."
"O Skanda, it has the luster of a blazing fire, is somewhat circular, and perfectly pure;
the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), who bestow prosperity, reside therein."
In the *Śrīparākhyatantra* it is also said:
"Śambara is [the presiding deity] of all vidyās, and likewise Īśvara is that which is called Ananta.
Therefore, above that is the Sadāśiva-tattva, presided over by Śiva who has entered into the state of office (*adhikārāvastha*).
It is the support of the world of Sadāśiva. As it is stated in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Now, above that, there shall be another auspicious reality consisting of all sovereignty, the supreme principle of Sadāśiva, pure like clear crystal," and so on.
"Therein dwells the Blessed Lord, Hara, the sovereign of all principles (tattvas),

the pervasive and omnipresent Sadāśiva, the supreme one whose form consists of mantra. Therefore, even above that, [the world] is presided over by this Śiva, who is free from activity and exists in a state of enjoyment.

The Śakti-tattva is said to be a specific transformation of the *bindu*, serving as the substratum for the four worlds consisting of the *nivṛtti* and other *kalās*. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"In the state of Sadāśiva, [the soul] possesses purified limbs and is delimited by the *sakala* and other [categories]."

"The Lord Sadāśiva is the master of the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, within the Bindu. Here, because it is presided over by Śiva— who exists in the state of enjoyment (bhoga) in the form of Sadyojāta and the others, as well as the masters of the kalās such as Nivṛtti— the term "Bindu" refers to the Śakti-tattva, which is the substratum of the worlds of the Bindu-kalā.
And it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Now, above that is the principle of the Bindu (baindava-tattva), which is stainless and faces in all directions.
And in the venerable Mataṅga:
"That which consists of the four forms, which is pure, and which is both with parts and without parts—
in that, the enjoyment of the Lord of the universe is declared to exist at all times."

Above that, the *bindu*— which is the supreme cause of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*)— is said to be "that which is to be purified by the supreme path" because it is the eternal object of governance for Paramaśiva in his state as the Guide (*nāyaka*), and because it is the power of his possession (*parigraha-śakti*).
Having presided over that, Śiva himself is called "Śiva" and "the state of Śiva" (*śivatva*) according to the etymological derivation of the Śiva-tattva.
That *bindu* is also designated by such terms as the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*), Mahāmāyā, Kuṇḍalinī, and so forth.
As it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "The reality beyond peace is the supreme principle, characterized by being imperishable and immutable.
And in the *Nādakārikās*: "The perfected Nāda is the supreme, the most auspicious Mālinī, Mahāmāyā."

It is stated in their respective scriptures that [the supreme reality] is designated by such various terms as *samanā*, *anāhata*, *bindu*, *aghoṣā*, *vācchadma*, *kuṇḍalī*, and the principle (*tattva*) called *vidyā*. Its effect is the world-sphere (*bhuvana*) beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*), which is presided over by Śiva in the form of Kevala-Īśāna.
Above that is the multitude of worlds consisting of the Kalās, beginning with Dhikā and ending with Nāda, which exist in a state of enjoyment;
and the Śakti-tattva, presided over by Śiva, is situated at its very summit. As it is stated in the venerable Mṛgendra:
"Indeed, even within the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), [the principles] belonging to the supreme Māyā..."
Those [deities] who are recited even in that [context] are also considered to be at the head of its creation.

Śiva, presiding over the world of the digits of sound (*nādakalā*), is called the Lord of Sound (*nādapati*). As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "The Lord is in the resonance of sound (*nāda*); He is the foremost among all possessors of power (*śakti*)."
(106) Furthermore,

the teachers maintain that these two principles known as Śakti and Śiva are to be purified on the path of *kalā* through the pervasion of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatītakalā*). As it is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati* regarding the pervasion of the *kalā* beyond peace:

"Both the Śakti-tattva and the Śiva-tattva are adorned with eight worlds," and so forth. Even in the *Ratnatraya*, the fifth [category] consists of the supreme Śiva-tattva, wherein there are fifteen cities (five times three). Thus, there is a distinction among the three mental principles (*manas-tattva*)—which are specific transformations of the *bindu* to be purified and which constitute the sentient substrate to be governed. This is the reality.

Thus, there is a distinction regarding that presiding Śiva here, such as being the "one who bestows grace" (*aupacādikabhedah*). As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra* and other texts: "However, he who exists within this division of the Lord (*pati*) in this scripture is like a division of the powers (*śakti*)."
"Through the metaphorical application of the distinction between functions, that distinction arises from the distinction of locations," and so forth.
"He is the qualified [practitioner], the enjoyer, and the one absorbed [in the Absolute], according to figurative usage.
And: "The Lord, Sadāśiva, and the Tranquil [Śiva] are distinguished by the difference in their functions.
And: "That distinction arises from the difference in function; there is no distinction in the ultimate sense."
Thus, for one whose self is bound, there are thirty-one impure *tattvas* to be purified, including *māyā*;

however, there are five pure ones, including *mahāmāyā*. Consequently, in initiation (*dīkṣā*), having performed the severing of the fetters (*pāśaccheda*) from above the *māyā-tattva* up to the end of the removal of impurity (*malaviccheda*), [the process continues] within the five *tattvas* beginning with Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).

Gradually, through the progressive intensification of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the manifestation of the Śiva-principle must be accomplished. Subsequently, however, by means of the cutting of the top-knot (*śikhāccheda*), the impelling nature of the concealing power (*tirodhānaśakti*)—which binds the fettered souls (*pāśa*)—is to be removed. This is for the purpose of establishing the state of Śiva that is to be attained; [this is done] within the Supreme Śiva, who is partless (*niṣkala*) and endowed with power free from all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).
(107) This Kuṇḍalinī does not abide as identical with the agent,
because she is the material cause, just as clay [abides] in the potter.

However, because that power of the inherent essence (*samaveta-śakti*) is one, the distinctions heard in the scriptures regarding its objects of knowledge, effects, and so forth, are merely figurative.
As it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The supreme power, established in the partless state, is inconceivable and faces in all directions."
Extremely subtle, stainless, eternal, infinite, and bestowing liberation.
She who unfolds within the principles and indeed within all principles—
by her, the entire world is sustained, appearing as both one and many forms.
And it is said in the *Mokṣakārikā* and other works:
"The power of the Wielder of the Trident is one alone, consisting of all knowledge and action.
"The single Śiva-power attains multiplicity through the assumption of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)."

And here, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara* and other texts, after stating the unity of the principles of Śakti and Śiva—which consist of the *bindu* and the *vidyā*—for the sake of purification through a single effort during the initiation into the principles (*tattvadīkṣā*), their union with Paramaśiva is taught. As it says in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "The principle of Śiva and so forth is not to be purified."
Having designated those three principles as the *sadāśivatattva* because they exist solely for that purpose and because there is no other presiding authority beyond their connection to Śiva,

and having established *paramaśiva*— the presider over the *bindu* and the purifier— as the *śivatattva*, the conjunction of the principles (*tattvasaṃyojana*) has been explained. As it is stated therein:
Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from affliction;
subtle, all-pervading, eternal, constant, imperishable, and sovereign.
Because it is the ultimate reality, it is immeasurable; because it is without characteristics, it is inexpressible.
Because it has no likeness, it is beyond comparison; because it is stainless, it is free from affliction.
It is subtle because it is imperceptible, and it is all-pervading because of its omnipresence.
It is eternal because it is devoid of a cause, and it is stable because it is immovable;
it is imperishable because of its perfection, and likewise it is the Lord because of its state as the sovereign master.
"This Śiva-tattva is proclaimed as situated above all paths.
And: "Then the Sadāśiva-tattva is situated in four stages.

It is precisely with this intention that, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, after not mentioning it at all in the division of the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), [it is discussed] in the context of the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*).
The name "Sadāśiva" is assigned to the triad of principles beginning with Sadāśiva. As it is stated in that very same [text]: "Beyond Īśāna and ending with Śānta, the principle is known as Sādāśiva;
its worlds also begin with Nāda, and there is no Lord other than Śiva."
"In that very place, within the dense [state] of withdrawal, the Vidyā eats the Sadātattva; its drop is the Bindu, and the resonance is the Dhvani.

The Supreme Power (Parāśakti) eats the Nāda, and she herself rules over the Śakti—thus is Hara. However, in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures, having described the distinctions of the states of dissolution and so forth of the presiding Lord Śiva by means of the three principles (*tattva*), [the text speaks] of the two things to be purified.

Having stated that Śakti and Śiva are included within the *bhoga-tattva*, while Sadāśiva-tattva and Īśvara-tattva are included within the *vicāra-tattva*, it has been explained that their unification occurs in Paramaśiva, whose nature consists in the state of the abode of the intellect (*buddhyālaya*).
In this same manner, the inclusion of others within [these categories] according to their respective [correspondences] should be understood in other tantras as well. And thus:

The non-contradiction of the *saṃhitās* and the authority of all scriptural statements are thus established; by this, their unity is proven. Otherwise, if one were to accept the meaning taught in one tantra while asserting the non-existence of the meaning taught in another tantra, [the system would collapse].

If the manifestation of the other form were not accepted, there would be no authority for any *saṃhitā*. This being the case, even though there is unity [among the scriptures], those who follow this or that particular *saṃhitā* must perform purification and the like during initiation according to the very sequence prescribed in that specific *saṃhitā*, just as they do for the daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and so forth; for it is traditionally held that a division of Tantras exists due to differences in ritual action (*kriyā*) and the like from the outset.
Therefore, in that case, one must act exactly as it has been stated, and not according to another system.

For it is only through initiation (*dīkṣā*)— which is preceded by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) consisting in the ripening of impurities (*malaparipāka*), which effects the severance of all fetters (*pāśa*) and the manifestation of Śiva-nature in all its objects— that the state of equality with the Supreme Lord is attained.

Supreme liberation is accomplished. As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* and other scriptures: "In the past, by the will of Śiva, the infinite power of Śiva (*śaivī*), which bestows the goals of Śiva, extended itself; that power [manifests] at the end of a person's birth."
From that union, his impurity—the cause of saṃsāra—flows away.
When that is exhausted, there arises for him the supreme, ultimate liberation.
Having approached a spiritual guide and been released from his bonds through initiation,
he proceeds to union with Śiva, stainless and free from all affliction.
"By this sequential yoga, having attained supreme isolation, because of being void of beginningless impurity, one does not undergo another existence. And:
"The initiated ones point toward the supremely peaceful state through the dissolution of the body."

Is it not the case that the state of Sadāśiva is attained through yoga, ritual conduct (*caryā*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and initiation (*dīkṣā*)? Or is liberation attained through the differentiation of the mind, or through the fourfold [path]? According to the venerable *Matanga-śruti*, these four—known as initiation, knowledge (*jñāna*), conduct, and yoga—are indeed equal in status.

(110) The means for attaining enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) are perceived [therein]. This is not so, however, because of a lack of understanding regarding the meaning of the sentence. For such is the meaning of that sentence: since the term "the state of Sadāśiva" (*sadāśivapada*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) there, it refers to the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the respective lords of those worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*).

Indeed, the attainment of those respective worlds occurs either through the connection with the fruit [of practice], or through conduct (*caryā*) consisting of the propitiation of that [deity], or through initiation (*dīkṣā*) consisting of the joining to those respective worlds, or through knowledge (*jñāna*)— which is a specific state of consciousness (*cittabheda*)— that is grounded in the form of the Lord of those respective worlds. It does not occur, however, by way of "equal conceptualization" (*samavikalpatā*), as will be explained later regarding knowledge and the other means, even when accompanied by initiation.

Because there is no authority [for practice] without it, she alone possesses primacy. Therefore, regarding the phrase "or liberation from the fourfold," the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*) is that liberation arises from this fourfold set when combined, whereas enjoyment (*bhoga*) does not arise from each individual part. For instance, in the case of conduct (*caryā*) and yoga, their very performance is not possible without knowledge.

For a yoga consisting of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and ritual conduct (*caryā*) is not possible when the object is unknown. Furthermore, it has been stated that even knowledge, being a substance, is incapable of effecting the liberation of persons from the bonds of impurity (*mala*) and so forth—just as an eye-physician's treatment is required for the eyes to be freed from cataracts. Therefore, initiation (*dīkṣā*) alone is the cause of liberation.

And it is said in that very same work, in another section: "Therefore, the practice of mantra is the primary means; through it, one attains enjoyment and liberation, even without a Lord [as an intermediary]. Also in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Initiation alone liberates and leads one upward to the abode of Śiva."
In the venerable *Ṣaṭsahasrikālottara*:
"Initiation alone bestows liberation upon the virtuous, being the cause for the manifestation of consciousness.
Furthermore, it is observed that knowledge and the other [perfections] are employed within initiation by means of the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the teacher.
As it is stated in that very *Śrīmanmataṅga*:
"One who is skilled in the *vidyāpāda*, who has mastered the sequence of the *kriyāpāda*,
who has practiced the *yogapāda*, and who follows the *caryāpāda*."

"One should perform the *gurudīkṣā*. This is solely for the purpose of removing the two impurities (*mala*)— those consisting of *māyā* and those pertaining to experience— without obstructing the enjoyment of those whose karmic effects have already begun, by means of the *sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*.

In this *Siddhāntasārasamuccaya*, which is a compendium of the essence of all the Āgamas, the text has reached its conclusion here. It is not known whether it is complete or incomplete. At the beginning, the title was given as *Siddhāntārthasamuccaya*; [this is determined] from observing the final line.
It is doubted whether [the work] might be titled *Siddhāntasārasamuccaya* or *Sakalāgamasārasaṃgraha*.
